Certificate of Formation: Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code Section 101.051 (Certain Provisions Contained in Certificate of Formation), read with Chapter 3, Subchapter C (general formation filing requirements applicable to all Texas entity types). CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 via Justia/Texas Legislature statute text.
Company Agreement (Operating Agreement): Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code Section 101.001(1) (definition of 'company agreement') and Section 101.052 (Company Agreement -- governs relations among members, managers, officers, and the company itself). CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 via Texas Legislature statute text (statutes.capitol.texas.gov).
Texas Business Organizations Code Chapte: Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code Title 3, Chapter 101 (Limited Liability Companies) -- the LLC-specific chapter, distinct from Chapter 21 (For-Profit Corporations) used for the corporation entity-type file.
Texas Franchise Tax Public Information R: Tex. Tax Code Section 171.203 (Public Information Report requirement), filed with the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts on Form 05-102 -- NOT a Secretary of State filing. CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 via the Comptroller's own site (comptroller.texas.gov) and multiple cross-checked secondary sources: Texas does not require a traditional Secretary-of-State annual report for LLCs or corporations; the PIR/franchise tax system is how that obligation is actually met. This corrects the framing used in the existing corporation.json's 'Annual Report Filing (Secretary of State)' entry, which was not updated as part of this file -- flagged separately for review, not changed here. IMPORTANT ADDITION 2026-08-30: an LLC only actually owes franchise tax once its annualized total revenue crosses the state's 'no tax due' threshold (currently $2.65 million). Below that threshold, no tax is owed, but the PIR must still be filed annually to keep the LLC in good standing -- filing and owing are two separate obligations, and this entry covers both.
Workers' Compensation Policy: Tex. Labor Code Section 406.002 -- Texas is the only state in the country where workers' compensation coverage is elective, not mandatory, for most private employers. An employer who opts out ('non-subscriber') must notify the Texas Division of Workers' Compensation (Section 406.004) and notify employees (Section 406.005), and forfeits certain common-law defenses in the event of a workplace injury lawsuit. EXCEPTION: coverage is mandatory for government building/construction contracts under Section 406.096. CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 across multiple independent sources; added retroactively as a batch correction across all deployed entity-type files that list this document type.
